title: Basics
content: =============================== echo -e "\n hello" • -e allows escape characters ================== stat [file|directory] • Shows stats, used to check hard link and Access, Modify, Change(AMC), and blocks(blocks are multiples of 8, when size reaches over 4096 block, the block will show 16) ================== cd [file|directory] • Change directory, (shell built in) ================== xxd [file] • Hexdump • Shows 3 cols(aka hexdump); memory, hexadecimal, human readable ascii, those 3 columns combined is called hexdump xxd -r [file] • reverse the hexdump to regular ascii and can be used with > to redirect output ================== pwd • print working directory ================== ls -lahi -AFC • a for all, l for list detail, h for human readable size, A for almost all but doesnt include . and .. , i for inodes, F for type tailing, C is used only for redirecting to files for horizontal format ls -a --sort name ================== Wildcards test?.txt [a-z].txt test[0-9].txt *.log • ? Any character, * any count of char, ~ for $HOME, e.g., ls test?.txt ================== cat -nAs [file] • n for line number, A for showing all including non printable characters, s for squeezing \n cat > [file] • > to overwrite and >> to append. ctrl + d to save and exit, ================== << (Heredoc) cat < [file] Name: someone EOF • Uhhh EOF can be replaced with anything ================== less [file] • pager, to read in page, can be piped to it to read in page too ================== head -n 5 [file] • n for line count , top 5 lines in this case ================== tail -f [file] tail -n +1 ./* • f for live following the last message like logs, n for line count, -n +1 is used for mentioning the file names when printing multiple files ================== grep -rivn -A 2 -B 2 "search_word" [file|dir] • r for recursive search used with directory, i for ignore case, v for invert, n for line number, A & B for including line after and before grep -C 3 -E "=+" data.gxt • C for including lines both before and after, E for expression, "=+" matches =, ===, or more, • "={2,}\s+\w+" 2 or more times of =, \s+ 1 or more spaces, \w+ 1 or more words ================== find . -name "logs" -type d • type d for directory, f for file find / -iname "*.log" -type f -user username -group groupname -size 33c -exec rm {} \; • -iname for case insensitive search, size c for bytes, +10M for more than 10 Megabytes, -1G for less than 1 Gigabyte • exec for execute on what it founds, {} placeholder, \; terminates cmd ================== locate [file|dir] • unlike find which crawls in hard drive storage, it searchs in /var/lib/mlocate/mlocate.db to locate extremely fast • Do "sudo updatedb" to renew db if new files aren't found ================== which -a [cmd] • a for search all. It searches the cmd listed in $PATH and shows the first found executable script with that name, because, by default if you execute a cmd it goes through $PATH from left to right. in short, it shows the path of cmd ================== type -ta [cmd|/path/to/cmd] • a for all including alias, t for printing only type(alias, shellbuiltin) used for shell scripting, a for all ================== whereis -l [cmd] • Just like which cmd, ignores $PATH, ignore symlinks to not get duplicate result, useful if $PATH is broken incase malicious users or anything, also used for getting man page's location • l for listing the hardcoded path whereis uses to search for, man: means it searches man pages in there ================== whatis [cmd] • One line explaining what the cmd does ================== string [file] • Extracts human readable texts (4 or more printable characters) ================== man [cmd] • manual page info [cmd] • more detailed then man with eg., but not all cmds support ================== apropos "search text" • searches man pages, output will look like grep, egrep and other cmds ================== --help --version • Most cmds have these options written in it ================== ln -s [target] [path/link name] • Soft link and hard link, -s for soft link ================== readlink -f [link] • shows where the link points to, f for follow link to the end and shows absolute path, yes f follows links ================== touch [file|/path/to/file] ================== mkdir -p dir1 dir2 /path/to/dir "my dir" • p creates path even if didnt exist ================== rm -rf file1.txt dir2 rmdir empty_dir • r for recrusive, f for force, rmdir only works for empty dir, ================== cp source.txt path/renamed_dest.txt cp -r docs/ source1.txt source2.txt dest/ • r for recursive ================== mv -iv [src(s)(file | dir)] [dest (file | dir)] • If dest doesnt exist it renames, -v for verbose, -i for confirmation incase overwrite, doesnt need -r ================== tee (99% used with pipe) echo "error: crash" | tee -a failure.log | grep "error" echo "10.0.0.5 prod" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts • tee pipes things. If no pipe at end to catch the stdout, then it will show in your terminal, -a is for appending. • often used for sudo tee because echo "write" >, the > doesnt have sudo perm ================== file [file] • Used to check the type of file like ascii text(your everyday normal text) or tar archived or zip with algorithm(gzip) =============================== Archiving(tar,..) & Compressing(gzip) tar -czvf [archive.tar.gz] [folder|file to tar] tar -cjvf [archive.tar.bz2] [path/to tar] tar -cJvf [archive.tar.xz] [specify what to tar] tar -xvf [archive.tar.gz] tar -tf or -tvf to view contents inside • c for archive, z for gzip(tar uses gzip), v for verbose, f for specifying file, j for bzip2, J for Xz, no zip for just archive, if the "file" cmd says its archived its probably tar • x for extract and modern linux automatically knows which type of zip to extract, itll unarchive and if its compressed, itll extract in one go ================== zip -r myfiles.zip /path/to/folder unzip myfiles.zip • Unlike tar, zip combines archiving and compression , is cross platform tool, so best use for using between Windows and Linux or such • r for recursive for dir, -e for encryption ================== gzip -k app.log gunzip app.log.gz • k for keep original and use copy ================== bzip2 -k app.txt bunzip2 app.txt.bz2 • k for keep original same as gzip =============================== 0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr > = 1> find /etc -name "*.conf" 2>/dev/null • 2> redirect error, no space after 2> cron_job.sh &> deployment.log • &> redirect success and error ================== cut -d ':' -f 1 /etc/passwd • delimiter, fields ================== sort -nrh names.txt • Numeric sort, reverse, human numeric(2K, 4M, 1G) ================== uniq -cd names.txt • Count, duplicates only, always with sort ================== tr (cannot use directly, must be piped|) echo "devops engineering" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' echo "DevOps and DevSecOps" | tr -s ' ' • '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' '[:alpha:]' '[:digit:]' '0-9' '[:punct]' '[:space:]' • -d for delete, -s for squeeze ================== wc -lwc -mL [file] • line count, word count, byte cout • -m character count, -L count of characters in the longest line • docker ps -q | wc -l ================== nl -n ln -v 1 [file|or redirected|] • -n ln for spacing , -n nl, -v starting no. ================== xargs -I {} • -I {} placeholder find . -name "*.log" | xargs -I {} mv {} /var/log/backup/ ls *.sh | xargs -I {} ln -s {} /usr/local/bin/{} echo "a b c" | xargs -n1 -I {} touch {}.txt find . -name "*.tmp" | xargs rm -f • Normal xargs attaches the output to the end {} can help in middle, -n1 uses one argument as a one line of cmd, -n2 and so on, whitespaces and newlines are its default delimiter ================== join -t ',' file1.csv file2.csv join -1 2 -2 1 file1.csv file3.csv • Merges first column of matchings, -t for defining delimiter • -1 for first file's column's number ================== echo "http://api.local" | sed 's/http/https/g' sed '/kube-system/d' cluster.log • s/ replace, /g global, /d is delete • -E extended regex, allows advanced regex ==================

title: Permissions and Proccesses
content: =============================== whoami • Shows current logged in user ================== id [can pass user] • -u for uid, -g for primary gid, -G for seondary group ids, pair those flags with -n for names ================== /etc/passwd /etc/group • Use these files to view users and groups, you have to only rely on this, no other cmd is reliable ================== sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash userA • -m for home directory, always leave -m alone, dont combine with other flags, -s for specifying default login shell, can use other shells like /usr/bin/false • -G secondarygroup1,group2, -g for primary group, -c for comment mostly used with describing what the bot does in automation ================== sudo passwd userA • After adding user you gotta assign password to let user able to login, or you can sudo su - userA, with sudo's password(current user), not root, and can change any user's password passwd • Can use without sudo for normal users to change their own password ================== sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh username • -s change default shell, -c for comment sudo usermod -d /home/newhome -m user sudo usermod -aG developers user • -d change home, -m moves content as well, -g for primary group,-a for append, -G for secondary groups ================== sudo usermod -L user sudo usermod -U user • Lock and unlock, modfies /etc/shadow , put ! infront - user:!$6$exAmPLePasS... • Used when user quits his job and leaves company ================== groups [can put username] • Shows all groups the user belongs to, and if you dont put any arg, itll print current user session's active groups, not the groups user belongs to ================== sudo groupadd -g 1500 engineergroup • -g for gid, no need to use -g, its use mostly for automation like with docker ================== sudo gpasswd -d username groupname • -d for removing group from a user,-a for add secondary group ================== sudo groupdel groupname • deletes group, cant delete if a group is primary to a user, bypasses secondary ================== sudo groupmod -n newname oldname • Mostly used for renaming groups sudo groupdel groupname • To del empty groups ================== su - [root|user] • Inlcuding - is login shell, without it is non-login shell, not specifying user mostly default to root. sudo -i • same as su -, but the password is strictly the root's password, if it doesnt work, try setting the root's password using "sudo passwd root" exit, whoami ================== chmod u+rw,g+r,o-rwx script.sh chmod +x script.sh chmod -R 755 /home/user/scripts • -R for recursive including dir, and dir have x by default to able to cd ================== sudo chown --reference=test.txt newfile.txt sudo chown owner:group file.txt • -R for recursive, strictly require sudo ================== umask -S (-S for symbolic) umask [022|0022|or else] • Files: 666-022 = 644 • Dirs: 777-022 = 755 ================== SUID | -rwsr-xr-x • Makes the script run as the owner of the file, shows s, if it is S, it means it didnt set x perm for the owner • chmod u+s file || chmod 4755 file.sh ================== SGID | drwxrwsr-x • Like SUID but runs with the group privilege, common to set on dirs since it would make the files created inside to automatically set the group to it. • chmod g+s dir || chmod 2775 sharedDir ================== STICKY BITS | drwxrwxrwt • Used only on directories, users can delete or rename the files only if they are the owner. /tmp has it. • chmod +t dir || chmod 1777 dir ================== ACLs | -rwxrwxrwx+ the + is ACL • heavily used in dirs, but acl is not used commonly, gives specific users or groups specific perm mount | grep acl • Checks if your device supports ACL, sometimes if it returns nothing, it still supports it getfacl [file] • shows ACL perm of the file setfacl -b [file] setfacl -m u:sarah:rw [file] • -m modifies,u: gives specific user read,write access, g: for group, -b clears, -x u:user for remove specific, -R for recursive for dir, -d dir for default apply ACLs to files in the dir apt install acl ================== mktemp -d • creates temp file in /tmp, -d means create directory =============================== Process management ================== ps echo $$ for current shell's PID ps aux | grep heart • ps show process, a all user, x includes procceses without terminal, u displays user info ================== top, htop • Live process ================== pgrep • pgrep python -> 14205, shows pid ================== kill killall (firefox|python) pkill • killall, if you have 5 python processes, itll kill all • pkill py wil kill python, pytest, etc. Numbers you should know: 1,9,15 • kill -15 (default) is polite, -9 (SIGKILL), -1 (SIGHUP) (sig hangup) reloads which tells to read the configs again and restart ================== sleep 30 & • Block terminal for 30 sec, & at end for background ================== jobs • Shows all jobs in current shell's session with job ids like [1] ================== fg %1 bg %1 • resumes job 1 to foreground(fg) and background(bg) CTRL + Z (SIGTSTP)( sig terminal stop) • Stops running process ================== nice -n 10 tar -czf backup.tar.gz /var/www sudo nice -n -5 python3 heavy_script.py • 19(lowest) to -20(highest) priority, requires sudo when using minus. sudo renice -n -20 -p 1234 sudo renice +10 -u john • -p is pid, -u makes all proccess of the user to +10 ps -eo pid,ni,comm to see nice values ===============================
